items.question: On the compass correction card shown in the FAA Pilot's Handbook, what compass heading should the pilot steer to fly a heading of 090 with the radios on, and with the radios off?
items.reference_answer: Steer 095 with the radios on and 094 with the radios off.
items.answer:
The compass correction card (Source 1) lists values for "FOR STEER" heading 090: with the radio on (RDO. ON), the compass reading is 095, and with the radio off (RDO. OFF), it is 094 [1].

So, to fly a heading of 090:
- Radio on: steer compass heading 095 [1]
- Radio off: steer compass heading 094 [1]

Each table has a header row labelled "FOR STEER" followed by heading columns, and two data rows labelled "RDO. ON" and "RDO. OFF" (radio on and radio off). Each value is a handwritten-style compass reading, and the card gives the steering heading and the resulting compass reading with radio on and off.

Top table, FOR STEER headings: 000, 030, 060, 090, 120, 150
- RDO. ON: 001, 032, 062, 095, 123, 155
- RDO. OFF: 002, 031, 064, 094, 125, 157

Bottom table, FOR STEER headings: 180, 210, 240, 270, 300, 330
- RDO. ON: 176, 210, 243, 271, 296, 325
- RDO. OFF: 174, 210, 240, 273, 298, 327

The card is a lookup table: for any steered heading, the corresponding RDO. ON or RDO. OFF value gives the magnetic compass indication to be read when the radio is on or off, reflecting radio-induced deviation. No units or axis labels beyond these row and column headers are shown.

Figure 8-35. A compass correction card shows the deviation correction for any heading.

Figure 16-12 is a compass deviation card, shown as a two-block table that maps magnetic headings (For) to compass steering headings (Steer). Top block, columns left to right: For (Magnetic) N, 30, 60, E, 120, 150; Steer (Compass) 0, 28, 57, 86, 117, 148. Bottom block, columns left to right: For (Magnetic S, 210, 240, W, 300, 330; Steer (Compass) 180, 212, 243, 274, 303, 332. Each column pairs a magnetic heading with the compass heading to steer to achieve it, so the deviation at each point is the difference between the two values (for example, N = 0 magnetic maps to 0 compass; 30 magnetic maps to 28 compass; E = 90 magnetic maps to 86 compass; S = 180 magnetic maps to 180 compass; W = 270 magnetic maps to 274 compass). The bottom block's first label is printed as 'For (Magnetic' without a closing parenthesis.

Figure 16-12. Compass deviation card.

Diagram (Figure 16-16 from FAA-H-8083-25C, Chapter 16 Navigation) showing the relationship between true, magnetic, and compass headings for a particular instance. A small aircraft is drawn in plan view (top-down) at lower center, nose pointing right, with a horizontal orange/tan arrow labeled "Heading" extending from its nose to the right. From a common origin point at the left, several vectors fan out upward and to the right, each curving toward the heading arrow: a red arrow labeled "TN" points straight up (true north reference line); a thin green line labeled "MN" (magnetic north) is near vertical, slightly clockwise of TN; a thin gray line labeled "CN" (compass north) lies just clockwise of MN. A yellow bracketed segment between TN and MN is labeled "VAR 10° E" (variation 10° east). A narrow bracket between MN and CN is labeled "DEV 4°" (deviation 4°). Three thick curved arrows originate from the origin and sweep to the heading arrow: a red arrow labeled "TH-088°" (true heading 088°), a green arrow labeled "MH-078°" (magnetic heading 078°), and a gray arrow labeled "CH-074°" (compass heading 074°). Each arrow terminates with an arrowhead pointing down toward the Heading arrow. Relationship: TH = MH + variation (78° + 10° E = 88°) and MH = CH + deviation (74° + 4° = 78°), with the arrows showing progressively smaller angles from true to magnetic to compass heading.

Figure 16-16. Relationship between true, magnetic, and compass headings for a particular instance.

Diagram from FAA Pilot's Handbook (Ch. 16 Navigation, Effect of Wind) illustrating wind correction angle. A light-blue block arrow labeled "Wind" points downward (from top toward the bottom) at the top left. A yellow horizontal line runs left to right labeled "Track" (beneath the middle airplane) and "Desired course" (right side), with a yellow arrowhead at the right end labeled "090°". A blue-and-white striped line labeled "Heading" extends from the left airplane's nose up and to the right, ending at the upper right with the label "075°" in blue. Three simplified airplane illustrations (white/blue, viewed from above/side) are drawn along the yellow track line, showing the aircraft nose angled toward the heading line (075°) while progressing along the track (090°). A double-headed dark red vertical arrow between the heading line and the track is labeled "Wind correction angle" (red text, split across three lines: "Wind", "correction", "angle"). Relationships: the desired course is 090°, the heading is 075°, and the wind correction angle is the angular difference between heading and track needed to counteract wind drift and keep the aircraft on the desired course. Background is a green gradient.

Figure 16-17. Establishing a wind correction angle that counteracts wind drift and maintains the desired course.

Because each aircraft has its own internal effect upon the onboard compass systems from its own localized magnetic influencers, the pilot must add or subtract these influencers based upon the direction he or she is flying. The application of deviation (taken from a compass deviation card) compensates the magnetic course unique to that aircraft’s compass system (as affected by localized magnetic influencers) and it now becomes the compass course. Therefore, the compass course, when followed (in a no wind condition), takes the aircraft from point A to point B even though the aircraft heading may not match the original course line drawn on the chart.

If the variation is shown as “9° E,” this means that MN is 9° east of TN. If a TC of 360° is to be flown, 9° must be subtracted from 360°, which results in a magnetic heading of 351°. To fly east, a magnetic course of 081° (090° – 9°) would be flown. To fly south, the magnetic course would be 171° (180° – 9°). To fly west, it would be 261° (270° – 9°). To fly a TH of 060°, a magnetic course of 051° (060° – 9°) would be flown.

Remember, if variation is west, add; if east, subtract. One method for remembering whether to add or subtract variation is the phrase “east is least (subtract) and west is best (add).”

verdict.rationale: The answer gives the reference values: 095 with the radios on and 094 with them off. Both values appear under the 090 column on the correction card.
